lead: At the oaks of Mamre Abraham runs to welcome three strangers in the heat of the day, and receives from them the promise that Sarah will have a son. Sarah laughs, and the Lord asks, “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?” In the Gospel a centurion, a Gentile, trusts that Jesus can heal his servant with a word, and Jesus heals Peter’s mother-in-law and many others. Instead of a psalm the Church sings Mary’s Magnificat, for Mary is the woman in whom God did the most wonderful thing of all, and who sang that God remembered his mercy, “according to the promise he made to our ancestors, to Abraham and to his descendants forever”.

r.h: Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
set: Abraham is camped by the oaks of Mamre near Hebron. In the desert world, hospitality to travellers was a sacred duty; a stranger might die without it. Abraham does more than his duty. He runs, bows, has water brought for their feet, and has a feast prepared.

The narrator tells us at once that “the Lord appeared to Abraham”, but Abraham sees three men. Through the story the text moves between “they” and “the Lord”, and the reader is left to wonder at the mystery.
str: vv. 1–2: the Lord appears; Abraham sees three men and runs to meet them.
vv. 3–8: the welcome: water, rest, bread, a calf, curds and milk.
vv. 9–10: “Where is your wife Sarah?” The promise of a son.
vv. 11–15: Sarah laughs; “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?”; Sarah’s fear and denial.
kw: Verbs of haste appear again and again: Abraham runs (rûṣ), hastens (mahar) to Sarah, runs to the herd, and the servant hastens. An old man in the midday heat rushes to serve.
Sarah laughs “to herself”, out of long disappointment. The same root gives the name Isaac. God does not punish her laughter; he answers it with a question and a promise.
From peleʾ, wonder, a deed beyond human power. The angel Gabriel will echo this to Mary: “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37).
vv: He looked up and saw three men standing near him.
Hebrews 13:2 recalls this scene: “by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it.”
Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.
Abraham promises “a little” and gives a great deal. True hospitality is generous and humble at once.
Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
The central verse. The question is addressed to Abraham and Sarah, and to every reader who has given up hope.
God is gentle with Sarah. He does not reject her; he simply tells her the truth. The promise stands.
ch: The Catechism says that the remarkable hospitality at Mamre is the prelude to the annunciation of the true Son of the promise (CCC 2571). Many Fathers, among them St Ambrose and St Augustine, saw in the three visitors a hint of the mystery of the Holy Trinity (in substance), and the famous icon by Andrei Rublev shows the three seated at Abraham’s table. The Church does not say that Abraham knew the Trinity; she says that God was already preparing his people to receive the full revelation of who he is.

set: Jesus enters Capernaum, the lakeside town where he made his home. A centurion, an officer in charge of about a hundred soldiers, comes to ask for help. Many scholars think he served Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, rather than a Roman legion; either way he was a Gentile. Matthew then adds two more healings, Peter’s mother-in-law and the sick brought at evening, and a fulfilment text from Isaiah.
str: vv. 5–9: the centurion’s request and his word of humble faith.
vv. 10–13: Jesus marvels at his faith; many will come from east and west; the servant is healed.
vv. 14–15: Peter’s mother-in-law is healed and serves him.
vv. 16–17: many are healed at evening; Isaiah 53:4 is fulfilled.
kw: A commander of a hundred men. In the Gospels and Acts centurions often appear in a good light: at the Cross (27:54) and Cornelius (Acts 10).
Literally “fit” or “sufficient”. The centurion knows that a Jew might not enter a Gentile’s house without becoming unclean, and he does not want to burden Jesus. His humility opens him to grace.
From the same root as diakonos, servant. The healed woman at once uses her restored strength to serve Jesus. Healing leads to service.
vv: Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof; but only speak the word, and my servant will be healed.

The Church has made these words her own. At every Mass, before Communion, the faithful say: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed.”
in no one in Israel have I found such faith.
Jesus marvels at a Gentile’s faith. This is a sign of the mission to the nations that the Gospel will open at its end (28:19).
many will come from east and west and will eat with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven,
The image of the great banquet of the nations, foretold in Isaiah 25:6. The patriarchs of Israel sit at that table with them.
He took our infirmities and bore our diseases.
Matthew quotes Isaiah 53:4, the song of the suffering servant. Jesus does not heal from a distance; he takes our weakness on himself, and in the end he will carry it to the Cross.
ch: The Catechism quotes the centurion’s words in its teaching on preparing for Holy Communion (CCC 1386). St Augustine praised the centurion: by calling himself unworthy he showed himself worthy, so that Christ entered not his walls but his heart (in substance, Sermon 62). The warning about “the heirs of the kingdom” (v. 12) is said in the manner of the prophets, to shake anyone who presumes on privilege; the Church hears it as addressed to Christians too (7:21–23). It is not a judgment on the Jewish people, whom God has not rejected (CCC 839; Nostra Aetate 4).

rite: On Saturdays in Ordinary Time, when no obligatory memorial falls, the Latin Church may keep the memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Today’s response, the Magnificat, fits it well: the Lord who asked Abraham “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?” fulfilled his promise to Abraham in Mary’s Son.
study: Abraham ran to serve strangers in the heat of the day. Whom can I welcome this week, at home or in the parish, as if I were welcoming the Lord?
I say the centurion’s words before every Communion. What does it mean for me to say “only say the word” and truly mean it?
